claim: A migratory bird with fuel stores composed of more omega-6 polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) expended 11% less energy during long-duration (6 hr) flights with no change in oxidative costs.
source: Here, we show that a migratory bird with fuel stores composed of more omega-6 polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) expended 11% less energy during long-duration (6 hr) flights with no change in oxidative costs
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from doubly labeled water measurements during 6-hour flights, as shown in Figure 2a and described in the Results section.

claim: The short-term energy savings from omega-6 PUFA came at the long-term cost of higher oxidative damage in the omega-6 PUFA-fed birds.
source: however, this short-term energy savings came at the long-term cost of higher oxidative damage in the omega-6 PUFA-fed birds.
evidence: This claim is supported by oxidative damage measurements (d-ROMs assay) showing higher oxidative damage in PUFA-fed birds regardless of flight-training, as shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Flying is very energetically costly compared to running or swimming.
source: Given that flying is very energetically costly compared to running or swimming (Butler, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Butler, 2016.

claim: During long-duration flights, birds expend energy at a rate >10 times above their basal metabolic rate (BMR).
source: During long-duration flights, birds expend energy at a rate >10 times above their basal metabolic rate (BMR) (Butler, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Butler, 2016.

claim: Tour de France riders have sustained metabolic rates of around five times BMR.
source: whereas among the most extreme and competent human endurance athletes - Tour de France riders - have sustained metabolic rates of around five times BMR (Hammond and Diamond, 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hammond and Diamond, 1997.

claim: Birds use fats as their primary fuel (about 95%) for high-intensity endurance exercise such as migratory flights.
source: Furthermore, birds use fats as their primary fuel (about 95%) for high-intensity endurance exercise such as migratory flights (Jenni and Jenni-Eiermann, 1998; Guglielmo, 2010; Guglielmo, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jenni and Jenni-Eiermann, 1998; Guglielmo, 2010; Guglielmo, 2018.

claim: Fats used by birds for endurance exercise are highly susceptible to oxidative damage.
source: and these fats are highly susceptible to oxidative damage (Skrip and McWilliams, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Skrip and McWilliams, 2016.

claim: Reactive pro-oxidant molecules can cause considerable cellular damage and affect performance, health and potentially longevity.
source: Regulating oxidative balance is important for all air-breathing organisms because reactive pro-oxidant molecules can cause considerable cellular damage and so affect performance, health and potentially longevity (Halliwell and Gutteridge, 1999; Lane, 2005; Cooper-Mullin and McWilliams, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Halliwell and Gutteridge, 1999; Lane, 2005; Cooper-Mullin and McWilliams, 2016.

claim: The fatty acid composition of diet has a predominant influence on that of the body-fat stores in vertebrates.
source: One of the more remarkable features of fat metabolism in vertebrates is that in general 'you are what you eat', that is the fatty acid composition of diet has a predominant influence on that of the body-fat stores (West and Meng, 1968; Thomas and George, 1975; West and Peyton, 1980; Phetteplace and Watkins, 1989; Pierce et al., 2004; Pierce and McWilliams, 2005; Price and Guglielmo, 2009; Ben-Hamo et al., 2011; Abbott et al., 2012; Pierce and McWilliams, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating this relationship.

claim: The stored fat of MUFA-fed birds was 75% 18:1 and 10% 18:2.
source: The stored fat (in the furcular region) of MUFA-fed birds was 75% 18:1% and 10% 18:2
evidence: This claim is supported by direct measurements of fatty acid composition shown in Figure 1 and Table 2.

claim: The stored fat of PUFA-fed birds was 60% 18:1 and 20% 18:2 and 18:3.
source: whereas that of PUFA-fed birds was 60% 18:1% and 20% 18:2 and 18:3
evidence: This claim is supported by direct measurements of fatty acid composition shown in Figure 1 and Table 2.

claim: The three fatty acids primarily composing the fat stores of hand-raised starlings (16:0, 18:1, 18:2) are the same three fatty acids that predominate in the fat stores of free-living passerines sampled during their migration.
source: Importantly, these three fatty acids primarily composing the fat stores of our hand-raised starlings (i.e. 16:0, 18:1, 18:2) are the same three fatty acids that predominate in the fat stores of free-living passerines sampled during their migration (Pierce and McWilliams, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pierce and McWilliams, 2005.

claim: The two experimental diets were isocaloric and composed of 42% carbohydrates, 23% protein, and 20% fat.
source: The two diets were isocaloric and composed of 42% carbohydrates, 23% protein, and 20% fat.
evidence: This claim is supported by the diet composition data presented in Table 1.

claim: PUFA-fed birds lost substantially less body mass during the 6 hr flight (7.04 ± 0.30%) compared to MUFA-fed birds (9.01 ± 0.41%).
source: As expected from the 11% energy savings, PUFA-fed birds lost substantially less body mass during the 6 hr flight (7.04 ± 0.30%) compared to MUFA-fed bird (9.01 ± 0.41%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by body mass measurements before and after the 6-hour flight, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: BMR measured 36–40 hr after the longest flight was similar for MUFA- and PUFA-fed birds.
source: However, we found that BMR measured 36–40 hr after the longest flight was similar for MUFA- and PUFA-fed birds (Figure 2b)
evidence: This claim is supported by respirometry measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: BMR was not influenced by flight-training.
source: and was not influenced by flight-training (Training x Diet interaction: F1,25 = 0.04, p=0.85; Training effect: F1,25 = 0.02, p=0.88; Diet effect: F1,25 = 0.61, p=0.44)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of BMR measurements comparing trained and sedentary birds.

claim: The 11% energy savings achieved by starlings composed of more essential omega-6 PUFA during long-duration flights is quite substantial compared to other performance-enhancing contexts for other organisms.
source: The 11% energy savings (Figure 2a) achieved by starlings composed of more essential omega-6 PUFA during long-duration flights is quite substantial compared to other performance-enhancing contexts for other organisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparisons to other organisms presented in the text, including E. coli, naked mole rats, and Tour de France riders.

claim: Mutant strains of E. coli bacteria that did not incur the biosynthetic costs of the amino acid tryptophan used 0.01% less energy than wild types.
source: For example, mutant strains of E. coli bacteria that did not incur the biosynthetic costs of the amino acid tryptophan used 0.01% less energy than wild types (Dykhuizen, 1978)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dykhuizen, 1978.

claim: Naked mole rats saved 2% of their energy budgets by not developing a visual system.
source: Naked mole rats which inhabit the dark world of borrows saved 2% of their energy budgets by not developing a visual system (Cooper et al., 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cooper et al., 1993.

claim: Differences in the energy costs of the top-placing elite athletes such as Tour de France riders are on the order of <5%.
source: Differences in the energy costs of the top-placing elite athletes such as Tour de France riders (Saris et al., 1989; Hammond and Diamond, 1997; Santalla et al., 2012) are on the order of <5%.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Saris et al., 1989; Hammond and Diamond, 1997; Santalla et al., 2012.

claim: High levels of essential omega-6 PUFA in muscle membrane phospholipids have been associated with improved endurance capacity in rats and humans.
source: In rats and humans, high levels of essential omega-6 PUFA in muscle membrane phospholipids have been associated with improved endurance capacity (Ayre and Hulbert, 1996; Ayre and Hulbert, 1997; Andersson et al., 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ayre and Hulbert, 1996; Ayre and Hulbert, 1997; Andersson et al., 1998.

claim: Maximum running speed in 30 species of mammals was positively correlated with the omega-6 fatty acid content in skeletal muscle phospholipids.
source: Maximum running speed, a short-term performance measure, in 30 species of mammals was positively correlated with the omega-6 fatty acid content in skeletal muscle phospholipids (Arnold et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arnold et al., 2015.

claim: Red-eyed vireos and White-throated sparrows with fat stores composed of more omega-6 PUFA (18:2) have improved performance during short-term intense exercise.
source: Our own recent work and that of colleagues confirmed that two different passerines (Red-eyed vireos [Vireo olivaceous], White-throated sparrows [Zonotrichia albicollis]) with fat stores composed of more omega-6 PUFA (18:2) have improved performance during short-term intense exercise (Pierce and McWilliams, 2005; Pierce et al., 2005; Price, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pierce and McWilliams, 2005; Pierce et al., 2005; Price, 2010.

claim: Yellow-rumped warblers with enriched omega-3 PUFA in their muscle phospholipids decreased muscle oxidative enzymes, although these changes in muscle metabolism were not associated with changes in flight performance.
source: Yellow-rumped warblers (Setophaga coronata) with enriched omega-3 PUFA in their muscle phospholipids decreased muscle oxidative enzymes, although these changes in muscle metabolism were not associated with changes in flight performance (Dick and Guglielmo, 2019a)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dick and Guglielmo, 2019a.

claim: Migratory birds with fat stores composed of more essential omega-6 PUFA had improved performance (i.e. less energy used per km) during endurance flights (6 hr, ca. 260 km) compared to birds composed of more MUFA.
source: our experimental results here demonstrate that migratory birds with fat stores composed of more essential omega-6 PUFA had improved performance (i.e. less energy used per km) during endurance flights (6 hr, ca. 260 km) compared to birds composed of more MUFA
evidence: This claim is supported by the doubly labeled water measurements of energy expenditure during 6-hour flights shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The enhanced performance of PUFA-fed birds is because of the signaling properties of omega-6 PUFA.
source: and a recent companion study (Carter et al., 2020) suggests that this is because of the signaling properties of omega-6 PUFA
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carter et al., 2020.

claim: Flight-training over more than 2 weeks did not affect baseline levels of oxidative damage.
source: Flight-training over more than 2 weeks did not affect baseline levels of oxidative damage (compare Pre-training and Recovery; Figure 3c)
evidence: This claim is supported by oxidative damage measurements at different time points shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Antioxidant capacity decreased in flight-trained but not sedentary birds.
source: while antioxidant capacity decreased in flight-trained but not sedentary birds (Figure 3b)
evidence: This claim is supported by antioxidant capacity measurements shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Plasma uric acid decreased over time in both trained and sedentary starlings.
source: and plasma uric acid decreased over time in both trained and sedentary starlings (Figure 3a; see Table 3 for detailed statistical results)
evidence: This claim is supported by uric acid measurements shown in Figure 3a and statistical results in Table 3.

claim: A long-duration flight on Day 15 was associated with increased plasma uric acid.
source: A long-duration flight on Day 15 (average flight times for PUFA: 161.6 ± 31.2 min, and MUFA: 180.2 ± 28.3 min) was associated with increased plasma uric acid (Figure 3a)
evidence: This claim is supported by uric acid measurements at different time points shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Uric acid is a product of protein metabolism in birds and also a potent antioxidant.
source: a product of protein metabolism in birds and also a potent antioxidant (Sautin and Johnson, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sautin and Johnson, 2008.

claim: A long-duration flight on Day 15 was associated with a reduction in plasma triglycerides.
source: and a reduction in plasma triglycerides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Birds fed more essential omega-6 PUFA had higher oxidative damage than MUFA-fed birds regardless of flight-training.
source: Regardless of flight-training, birds fed more essential omega-6 PUFA had higher oxidative damage than MUFA-fed birds (main effect of flight; Figure 3c)
evidence: This claim is supported by oxidative damage measurements shown in Figure 3c.

claim: There is a fundamental oxidative cost of being composed of more polyunsaturated fatty acids.
source: suggesting a fundamental oxidative cost of being composed of more polyunsaturated fatty acids
evidence: This claim is inferred from the higher oxidative damage observed in PUFA-fed birds.

claim: An increase in activity may increase production of ROS in excess of the immediate capacity of antioxidants to quench them.
source: Animals performing exercise such as birds during a long-duration flight, and those that rely on large amounts of fat as fuel such as migratory birds, are especially prone to oxidative stress because (1) an increase in activity may increase production of ROS in excess of the immediate capacity of antioxidants to quench them
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about oxidative stress during exercise.

claim: Stored and structural fats, particularly PUFAs, are especially vulnerable to oxidative damage because of their chemical structure, and may generate their own variety of pro-oxidants.
source: and (2) stored and structural fats, particularly PUFAs, are especially vulnerable to oxidative damage because of their chemical structure, and may generate their own variety of pro-oxidants (Cooper-Mullin and McWilliams, 2016; Skrip and McWilliams, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cooper-Mullin and McWilliams, 2016; Skrip and McWilliams, 2016.

claim: Birds were capable of contending with the oxidative costs associated with a given flight.
source: Importantly, we found no significant change in oxidative damage or oxidative capacity immediately after flights (compare Post-flight to Pre-training and Recovery in Figure 3) suggesting that birds were capable of contending with the oxidative costs associated with a given flight.
evidence: This claim is supported by oxidative status measurements at different time points shown in Figure 3.

claim: Migratory birds pay the oxidative costs of being composed of more polyunsaturated fatty acids (primarily 18:2 and 18:3) over the long-term (e.g. migration period of the annual cycle) while gaining some energy savings only during a given migratory flight.
source: Instead, migratory birds pay the oxidative costs of being composed of more polyunsaturated fatty acids (primarily 18:2 and 18:3) over the long-term (e.g. migration period of the annual cycle) while gaining some energy savings only during a given migratory flight.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of oxidative damage (higher in PUFA birds regardless of flight) and energy savings (only during flight) observed in the experiments.

claim: Migratory birds that consume diets with more essential omega-6 PUFA (18:2) can substantially enhance their exercise performance (i.e. expend less energy) during long-duration flights without incurring increased self-maintenance (BMR) costs.
source: Given that fat composition of diet largely determines that of fat stores, migratory birds that consume diets with more essential omega-6 PUFA (18:2) can substantially enhance their exercise performance (i.e. expend less energy) during long-duration flights without incurring increased self-maintenance (BMR) costs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the energy expenditure and BMR measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Enhanced performance during flights has longer-term costs in terms of increased oxidative damage when fat stores are composed of more PUFA.
source: However, this enhanced performance during flights has longer-term costs in terms of increased oxidative damage when fat stores are composed of more PUFA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the oxidative damage measurements shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Migratory songbirds carefully discriminate between diets that differ only in their fatty acid composition.
source: Cafeteria-style diet choice experiments with migratory songbirds have shown that birds carefully discriminate between diets that differ only in their fatty acid composition (Pierce et al., 2004; Pierce and McWilliams, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pierce et al., 2004; Pierce and McWilliams, 2014.

claim: Migratory songbirds on average prefer to consume a composite diet that contains a 1:2 ratio of 18:2 to 18:1.
source: and on average prefer to consume a composite diet that contains a 1:2 ratio of 18:2 to 18:1 (Pierce and McWilliams, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pierce and McWilliams, 2014.

claim: Birds may choose among diets to optimize the trade-off between enhanced flight performance (more 18:2), while reducing the long-term costs of being composed of more long-chain PUFA.
source: This indicates that birds may choose among diets to optimize the trade-off between enhanced flight performance (more 18:2), while reducing the long-term costs of being composed of more long-chain PUFA.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed diet preferences and the trade-offs demonstrated in the study.

claim: Seasonal changes in fatty acid composition are commonly observed in migratory birds.
source: such seasonal changes in fatty acid composition are commonly observed in migratory birds (Pierce and McWilliams, 2005; Santalla et al., 2012; Pierce and McWilliams, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pierce and McWilliams, 2005; Santalla et al., 2012; Pierce and McWilliams, 2014.

claim: European starlings are common migratory birds in western Europe.
source: We used hand-raised European starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) from southern Germany (n = 95 total) for this two-part study because starlings are common migratory birds in western Europe (Feare, 1984)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feare, 1984.

claim: European starlings have been successfully hand-raised and trained to fly in windtunnels.
source: and they have been successfully hand-raised and trained to fly in windtunnels (Engel et al., 2006a)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Engel et al., 2006a.

claim: European starlings from the southeastern German population are medium-distance diurnal migrants that leave for wintering grounds in October and November and return to their Bavarian breeding grounds in April.
source: European starlings from this southeastern German population are medium-distance diurnal migrants that leave for wintering grounds in October and November and return to their Bavarian breeding grounds in April (Bairlein, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bairlein, 2014.

claim: Migratory distances for the southeastern German starling population vary from many hundreds of kilometers to several thousand kilometers, with some individuals overwintering in the Euro-Mediterranean region and others in northwest Africa.
source: Migratory distances for this population vary from many hundreds of kilometers to several thousand kilometers, with some individuals overwintering in the Euro-Mediterranean region and others in northwest Africa (Bairlein, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bairlein, 2014.

claim: The 6 hr duration of the final longest flight (6 hr, 260 km) was sufficiently long to provide adequate turnover of the isotope-labeled water and so ensure accurate measurements of energy expenditure using the doubly labeled water (DLW) technique.
source: The duration of the final longest flight (6 hr, 260 km) was sufficiently long to provide adequate turnover of the isotope-labeled water and so ensure accurate measurements of energy expenditure using the doubly labeled water (DLW) technique (Speakman, 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Speakman, 1997.

claim: The 6 hr duration of flight is within the range of typical single-day migratory flights for many free-living songbirds including starlings.
source: The 6 hr duration of flight is also within the range of typical single-day migratory flights for many free-living songbirds including starlings (Feare, 1984; Newton, 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Feare, 1984; Newton, 2006.

claim: The doubly labeled water method has been previously validated by comparison to indirect calorimetry in a range of small mammals.
source: This method has been previously validated by comparison to indirect calorimetry in a range of small mammals (Speakman and Król, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Speakman and Król, 2005.

claim: A single-pool model was used to calculate rates of CO2 production as recommended for use in animals less than 5 kg in body mass.
source: A single-pool model was used to calculate rates of CO2 production as recommended for use in animals less than 5 kg in body mass (Speakman, 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Speakman, 1993.

claim: Empirically measured variation in the amount of stored fat or protein used as fuel (as reflected in the RQ) results in errors in estimates of energy expenditure not exceeding ±2%.
source: Empirically measured variation in the amount of stored fat or protein used as fuel (as reflected in the RQ) results in errors in estimates of energy expenditure not exceeding ±2% (Black et al., 1986; Schmidt-Wellenburg et al., 2008; Westerterp, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Black et al., 1986; Schmidt-Wellenburg et al., 2008; Westerterp, 2017.

claim: The macronutrient composition of the two semi-synthetic diets simulates a natural high-lipid fruit diet.
source: The macronutrient composition of the two semi-synthetic diets simulates a natural high-lipid fruit diet (Johnson et al., 1985; Smith et al., 2007a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 1985; Smith et al., 2007a.

claim: The primary fatty acids in the experimental diet (>90% 16:0, 18:1, and 18:2) are also the most common fatty acids in natural fruits.
source: and the primary fatty acids in the diet (>90% 16:0, 18:1, and 18:2) are also the most common fatty acids in natural fruits (Pierce and McWilliams, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pierce and McWilliams, 2014.

claim: The primary fatty acids in the experimental diet are also the most common fatty acids in songbirds that eat fruits during migration.
source: and in songbirds that eat fruits during migration (Pierce and McWilliams, 2005; Pierce and McWilliams, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pierce and McWilliams, 2005; Pierce and McWilliams, 2014.

claim: European starlings switch to eating largely fruits during fall migration.
source: European starlings are like many fall-migrating songbirds in that they switch to eating largely fruits (Feare, 1984)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feare, 1984.

claim: For Experiment I, 36 starlings were flight-trained of which 33 completed their 6 hr long-duration flight (16 fed the MUFA diet, 17 fed the PUFA diet).
source: For Experiment I, we flight-trained 36 starlings of which 33 completed their 6 hr long-duration flight (16 fed the MUFA diet, 17 fed the PUFA diet).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: For Experiment II, there were 19 MUFA-fed birds (11 flight-trained, eight sedentary) and 17 PUFA-fed birds (nine flight-trained, eight sedentary).
source: For Experiment II, we added 1–2 untrained, sedentary (control) starlings in each training cohort which resulted in a total of 19 MUFA-fed birds (11 flight-trained, eight sedentary) and 17 PUFA-fed birds (nine flight-trained, eight sedentary).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The fatty acid composition of furcular fat from birds fed MUFA diets was significantly different from that of birds fed PUFA diets, in 18:1, 18:2, and 18:3 fatty acids.
source: Fatty acid composition (% ± SE) of furcular fat from birds fed MUFA diets was significantly different from that of birds fed PUFA diets, in 18:1, 18:2, and 18:3 fatty acids.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fatty acid composition data presented in Table 2.

claim: Flight-training resulted in increased plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate in trained birds compared to sedentary birds.
source: β-Hydroxybutyrate
evidence: This claim is inferred from Figure 3—figure supplement 1a showing higher beta-hydroxybutyrate levels in trained birds.

claim: PUFA-fed birds had higher plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate than MUFA-fed birds.
source: β-Hydroxybutyrate
evidence: This claim is inferred from Figure 3—figure supplement 1a showing the main effect of diet on beta-hydroxybutyrate.

claim: The long-duration flight on Day 15 resulted in increased plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate.
source: β-Hydroxybutyrate
evidence: This claim is inferred from Figure 3—figure supplement 1a showing higher beta-hydroxybutyrate at Post-flight compared to Recovery.

claim: The long-duration flight on Day 15 resulted in decreased plasma triglycerides.
source: Triglycerides
evidence: This claim is inferred from Figure 3—figure supplement 1b showing lower triglycerides at Post-flight compared to Recovery.
